opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think it comes down to freedom: the freedom to pick problems that I believe matter over the long term, even if they don't have an obvious payoff in the next quarter or the next year.

During my PhD I had the chance to build things like XGBoost and later TVM. What I found most rewarding wasn't just writing a paper. It was seeing a community form around an idea. People I'd never met started using the tools, contributing back, and pushing them in directions I hadn't imagined. A university is a very natural home for that kind of open, long-horizon work. You can start something a bit crazy, like rethinking how machine learning compilers should work, and you have the space to iterate on it for years.

The other big part is the students. Working with students is a little like building a system. You're not just solving one problem. You're helping people grow into researchers who will go on to solve many problems I'd never get to myself. That multiplier effect is something I really value.

I also like being able to sit at the intersection of things. In machine learning systems you have to care about algorithms, hardware, and software engineering all at once. Academia lets me collaborate across those boundaries, and also work closely with industry when it makes sense, without being locked into one product roadmap.

So it wasn't that I ruled out other paths. Industry is doing amazing work. But a faculty position gave me the combination I wanted most: the freedom to explore, the ability to build in the open, and the chance to work with brilliant young people.

r001.rationale: The response cites freedom to pursue long-term problems, build open communities, and mentor students. It does not identify enjoyment of uncertainty as a motivation.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, it wasn't a single moment, it was more of a gradual realization about what I enjoy doing.

During my PhD at the University of Washington, I spent a lot of time building things like XGBoost and MXNet, and later TVM. What I noticed was that the part I loved most wasn't just getting a system to work. It was the process of figuring out the right abstractions, and then watching other people pick those ideas up and take them in directions I never expected. A faculty position felt like the place where that kind of long-horizon, open-ended work is actually the job description rather than a side effect.

The second thing is students. I had great mentors, people like Carlos Guestrin, who gave me a lot of freedom and trust, and I wanted to be able to do that for others. There's something special about working with a student who starts out unsure, and a couple of years later they're teaching you things. You don't get that in quite the same way elsewhere.

And the third piece is that the problems I care about, machine learning systems, compilers, making models run efficiently everywhere, sit right at the intersection of research and real-world deployment. Academia lets me pursue the fundamental questions, while still staying close to open source and industry. I never wanted to pick one or the other, and a faculty role, at least the way I try to do it, lets me keep a foot in both worlds.

r001.rationale: The response says Chen enjoys open-ended, long-horizon work and seeing others take his ideas in unexpected directions, but it does not clearly identify enjoyment of uncertainty as a reason for choosing faculty.

astra-6.text: What drew me to a faculty career was the opportunity to pursue long-term research questions and work with students. I enjoy building things, but I also enjoy the process of figuring out what’s worth building—what questions matter and where a new approach could make a difference. A faculty role gives me room to explore those questions while helping students develop their own ideas and become independent researchers. That combination is really appealing to me.
